paras: The lynching of George Washington was the hanging by a mob of a Black man from Lincoln, New Mexico Territory, reported in June 1882. The only account found connects his death to his having eloped with a Mexican girl, and gives no date, place or names of the mob.

According to a brief in the Omaha Daily Bee, George Washington, described as "a Lincoln negro," eloped with a Mexican girl. "He died soon after—hung by a mob," the item continued, without saying where or when he was hanged or who made up the mob. The brief does not make clear whether "Lincoln" referred to the town or to Lincoln county, which the same column mentioned in another New Mexico item.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage found.

The Omaha Daily Bee ran the item on June 23, 1882, on page 4, in a column of territorial news briefs arranged under headings for Idaho, Montana, Oregon, California, Arizona and New Mexico. Under the "NEW MEXICO" heading the hanging appeared as a two-sentence note between an item on the territory's convicts and one on salt supplied from Lincoln county, with no headline and no comment. The paper named the victim's race and the girl's nationality but neither condemned nor justified the mob, and no other white paper carrying the story was found.
